Fix an arm \(a\), an atom \(s\in S_a\), a cell \(e\in E\) with \(e_a=s\), and put
\[
 w=\sum_{b\ne a}z_{be_b},\qquad g=-2w\in G_{as}.
\]
The defining properties of the declared dual potential give
\[
 u_{as}+\sum_{b\ne a}u_{be_b}=(z_{as}+w)^2
\]
and, after replacing only coordinate \(a\) by any \(t\in S_a\),
\[
 u_{at}+\sum_{b\ne a}u_{be_b}\le (z_{at}+w)^2.
\]
Subtracting and using \(\phi_{ar}=z_{ar}^2-u_{ar}\) yields
\[
 \phi_{at}-\phi_{as}
 \ge -2w(z_{at}-z_{as})
 =g(z_{at}-z_{as}).
\]
This proves the first assertion for every \(g\in G_{as}\).  Every marginal atom has positive multiplicity, so it is incident to a positive cell of \(q^\star\); hence each \(G_{as}\) is nonempty.

Suppose \(z_{as}<z_{at}\), and write \(d=z_{at}-z_{as}>0\).  Applying the preceding inequality first from \(s\) to \(t\), and then from \(t\) to \(s\), gives, for every \(g\in G_{as}\) and \(h\in G_{at}\),
\[
 gd\le \phi_{at}-\phi_{as}\le hd,
 \qquad
 g\le \frac{\phi_{at}-\phi_{as}}{z_{at}-z_{as}}\le h.
\]
In particular \(\max G_{as}\le\min G_{at}\), and therefore
\[
 z_{as}+\max G_{as}<z_{at}+\min G_{at}.
\]
Thus the closed intervals \(I_{as}\) are strictly ordered by \(z_{as}\) and pairwise disjoint within an arm.  The coordinate ranges implied by \(c=(1/4,1/4,-1/2)\) are
\[
 z_1,z_2\in[0,1/4],\qquad z_3\in[-1/2,0].
\]
Consequently
\[
 G_{1s},G_{2s}\subset[-1/2,1],\qquad G_{3s}\subset[-1,0],
\]
so \(I_{1s},I_{2s}\subset[-1/2,5/4]\) and \(I_{3s}\subset[-3/2,0]\), all within \([-2,2)\).

Finally suppose that \(I_{as}\) and \(I_{at}\) are contained in a common interval \(J\) of length \(H\).  If \(s=t\), both claimed quantities vanish.  If \(z_{as}<z_{at}\), choose \(g\in G_{as}\) and any \(h\in G_{at}\).  Slope ordering gives \(h-g\ge0\), while the two points \(z_{as}+g,z_{at}+h\in J\) satisfy
\[
 (z_{at}-z_{as})+(h-g)
 =(z_{at}+h)-(z_{as}+g)\le H.
\]
Hence both nonnegative summands are at most \(H\), and the secant bounds imply
\[
 |z_{at}-z_{as}|\le H,\quad
 0\le \phi_{at}-\phi_{as}-g(z_{at}-z_{as})
 \le(h-g)(z_{at}-z_{as})\le H^2.
\]
The case \(z_{at}<z_{as}\) is identical after reversing the order: if \(m\) is the secant slope, then \(h\le m\le g\) for \(h\in G_{at}\), and the remainder equals \((g-m)(z_{as}-z_{at})\).  Exact dyadic-boundary contact changes only whether an interval is declared a singleton; it does not alter any displayed inequality.  This proves all claims, including repeated observations after their aggregation into a single atom.

Put \(D_\ell=2^\ell\), so the dyadic partition of \([-2,2)\) has \(D_\ell\) cells of width \(h_\ell=4/D_\ell\).  There is at most one nonsingleton cluster per dyadic cell.  Moreover, strict disjointness from lem:ordered-dual-slopes implies that each of the \(D_\ell-1\) interior boundaries is crossed by at most one atom interval.  Assigning a crossing interval to, for example, its leftmost crossed boundary injects the set of crossing intervals into the set of boundaries.  Therefore
\[
 K_{a,\ell}:=|\mathcal P_{a,\ell}|
 \le D_\ell+(D_\ell-1)
 =2D_\ell-1<\frac8{h_\ell}.
\]
The partitions are nested.  Indeed, two atoms grouped at depth \(\ell+1\) have intervals contained in the same fine dyadic cell and hence in its unique parent cell at depth \(\ell\); a singleton block refines every block containing it.  At depth zero all support intervals lie in the single root cell \([-2,2)\), so \(K_{a,0}=1\).

Because each \(S_a\) is finite, the minimum positive distance between distinct \(z\)-atoms, when such a pair exists, is positive.  Choose \(L\) with \(h_L\) smaller than every such distance.  If two distinct atoms belonged to one nonsingleton block at depth \(L\), lem:ordered-dual-slopes would give \(|z_{at}-z_{as}|\le h_L\), a contradiction.  Thus \(\mathcal P_{a,L}\) is the singleton partition.  For rational input of total bit length \(B\), a nonzero difference of input rationals is at least \(2^{-O(B)}\), so one may take \(L=O(B)\).  Boundary-crossing intervals are already singletons, so ties with dyadic boundaries cause no exception.

We now justify the freezing operation without an unproved discrepancy assertion.  At a fixed depth let \(A_\ell\) be the zero--one incidence matrix whose rows are the clusters in the three arm partitions and whose columns are the currently available cells.  The current residual table is a nonnegative rational solution of
\[
 A_\ell q=b_\ell,
\]
where \(b_\ell\) is the original integer cluster-margin vector minus already frozen integer counts.  Thus \(b_\ell\) is entrywise nonnegative and integral.  If the positive columns of a feasible \(q\) are linearly dependent, choose a nonzero rational vector \(d\), supported on those columns, with \(A_\ell d=0\).  Since summing the rows for any one arm gives the all-ones row, \(\sum_e d_e=0\); hence \(d\) has both signs.  With
\[
 \varepsilon=\min_{e:d_e>0}\frac{q_e}{d_e},
 \]
the table \(q-\varepsilon d\) is feasible, nonnegative, and has strictly smaller positive support.  Repetition terminates with a basic feasible table.  The sums of the row blocks belonging to the three arms coincide, giving two row dependencies, and hence this table has at most
\[
 \operatorname{rank}(A_\ell)\le \sum_{a=1}^3K_{a,\ell}-2
\]
positive entries whenever its total mass is positive.

Freeze \(\lfloor q_e\rfloor\) copies of every positive cell.  All remaining cell masses lie in \([0,1)\).  Their total \(R_\ell\) is an integer because it is any arm's total residual cluster margin.  If the current table is zero, then \(R_\ell=0<24/h_\ell\).  Otherwise, counting the positive entries before freezing gives
\[
 R_\ell<\#\{e:q_e>0\}
 \le\sum_aK_{a,\ell}-2
 <\frac{24}{h_\ell}.
\]
At the root, \(K_{a,0}=1\) for all arms and \(A_0\) has rank one.  A basic table has at most one positive entry, equal to the integral total residual mass, so freezing its integer part leaves \(R_0=0\).  The frozen multiset therefore contains exactly \(N\) cells of the original support \(E\).

It remains to repair each arm's atom counts.  Independently for arm \(a\), match equal selected and required atoms at the leaves.  At each parent block match the unmatched selected occurrences from its children to the unmatched required occurrences from its children, and pass the imbalance upward.  Equality of root totals makes the final matching a bijection.  Fix a nonterminal depth \(\ell\), and inspect the state just after depth \(\ell+1\) was frozen.  For \(B\in\mathcal P_{a,\ell+1}\), let \(f_B\) be the already frozen count, \(r_B\) the current fractional residual margin, and \(l_B\) the number ultimately frozen at coarser levels.  Feasibility and construction give
\[
 \operatorname{original}(B)=f_B+r_B,\quad
 \operatorname{selected}(B)=f_B+l_B,\quad
 \sum_Br_B=\sum_Bl_B=R_{\ell+1}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 \frac12\sum_B|\operatorname{selected}(B)-\operatorname{original}(B)|
 =\frac12\sum_B|l_B-r_B|
 \le R_{\ell+1}.
\]
After all possible matches inside the depth-\(\ell+1\) blocks, the unmatched counts are exactly these signed discrepancies.  The number \(M_{a,\ell}\) of matches crossing children of a depth-\(\ell\) parent is their total positive discrepancy, bounded by the preceding half \(\ell^1\)-distance.  Hence
\[
 M_{a,\ell}\le R_{\ell+1}.
\]
Applying the three armwise bijections to the selected rows produces exactly the original marginal multiplicities, so the output belongs to \(\mathcal S_N(F)\).  Atom aggregation handles repetitions, and all operations above use exact comparisons, so arbitrarily small rational gaps and boundary contacts affect only \(L\), not any count bound.

Consider one frozen support row \(z=(z_1,z_2,z_3)\in E\), its repaired row \(z'=z+\delta\), and define
\[
 S=\sum_a z_a,\quad D=\sum_a\delta_a,\quad
 g_a=-2\sum_{b\ne a}z_b=-2(S-z_a)\in G_a(z_a).
\]
Dual tightness at \(z\) says \(S^2=\sum_a u_a(z_a)\), and \(u_a(r)=r^2-\phi_a(r)\).  Direct expansion therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 C(z')-\sum_a u_a(z'_a)
 &= (S+D)^2-\sum_a(z_a+\delta_a)^2+\sum_a\phi_a(z'_a)\\
 &=D^2-\sum_a\delta_a^2
   +\sum_a\{\phi_a(z'_a)-\phi_a(z_a)-g_a\delta_a\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the asserted exact identity.  Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 D^2-\sum_a\delta_a^2\le 2\sum_a\delta_a^2.
\]
If a nonzero arm-\(a\) movement has lowest common partition block at depth \(\ell\), that block is nonsingleton and both atom intervals lie in one dyadic cell of width \(h_\ell\).  Lem:ordered-dual-slopes, applied with the actual support slope \(g_a\), gives
\[
 \delta_a^2\le h_\ell^2,\quad
 0\le\phi_a(z'_a)-\phi_a(z_a)-g_a\delta_a\le h_\ell^2.
\]
Thus the contribution of that coordinate to the upper bound is at most \(3h_\ell^2\); a singleton or unmoved coordinate contributes zero.

Sum over all \(N\) rows.  Repair preserves every marginal multiplicity, so
\[
 \sum_{\text{rows}}\sum_a u_a(z'_a)
 =\sum_{a,s}b_{as}u_{as}
 =N V_{\mathrm{rel}}(F),
\]
where the last equality is dual optimality for \(q^\star=N\pi^\star\).  Lem:hierarchical-repair then yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
 N\{C_{\mathrm{alg}}(F)-V_{\mathrm{rel}}(F)\}
 &\le 3\sum_{a=1}^3\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}h_\ell^2M_{a,\ell}\\
 &\le 9\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}h_\ell^2R_{\ell+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(R_{\ell+1}<24/h_{\ell+1}=48/h_\ell\),
\[
 9\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}h_\ell^2R_{\ell+1}
 <432\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}h_\ell
 <432\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}4\,2^{-\ell}
 =3456.
\]
If \(L=0\), there is no movement and the sums are empty.  This proves the claimed accounting and its strict universal bound.

Apply def:rounding-algorithm and lem:hierarchical-repair to an optimal coupling \(\pi^\star\).  The output \(T_{\mathrm{alg}}\) lies in \(\mathcal S_N(F)\), and lem:quadratic-slack-accounting gives
\[
 C_{\mathrm{alg}}(F)<V_{\mathrm{rel}}(F)+\frac{3456}{N}.
\]
Every realizable schedule induces a coupling in \(\Gamma(F)\), while \(T_{\mathrm{alg}}\) is feasible for def:realizable-value.  Hence
\[
 V_{\mathrm{rel}}(F)\le V_{\mathrm{int}}(F)
 \le C_{\mathrm{alg}}(F)
 <V_{\mathrm{rel}}(F)+\frac{3456}{N}.
\]
Also \(0\le C(y)\le1/4\), because \(\sum_ac_ay_a\in[-1/2,1/2]\).  It follows that
\[
 0\le V_{\mathrm{int}}(F)-V_{\mathrm{rel}}(F)
 \le\min\left\{\frac14,\frac{3456}{N}\right\}.
\]

For the complexity assertion, let the rational input bit length be \(B\).  Aggregating and sorting at most \(N\) atoms per arm is polynomial.  The support \(E\) has at most \(N^3\) cells, and each \(G_{as}\) is obtained by scanning that support.  The separation argument in lem:hierarchical-repair gives \(L=O(B)\), and dyadic cell indices are computed directly from rational endpoints rather than by materializing a grid.

At each depth the basic-table step is implemented by the support-elimination construction in lem:hierarchical-repair.  Rational Gaussian elimination supplies an integral kernel vector after clearing denominators; its coordinates are minors of a zero--one matrix and therefore have polynomial bit length by the Leibniz determinant bound.  If the current table has common denominator \(D\), one elimination multiplies a common denominator by at most one such kernel coordinate.  There are at most \(N^3\) eliminations per depth, so the accumulated bit length is polynomial in \(N+B\).  Exact rational addition, multiplication, comparison, and Gaussian elimination consequently give polynomial bit complexity.  Freezing expands at most \(N\) rows.  The three tree matchings use at most \(O(NL)\) occurrence moves.  Thus the whole deterministic construction is polynomial in \(N\) and \(B\).

Finally, label the output rows by their arm-1 occurrences.  Since each output column has exactly the prescribed occurrence multiset, the arm-2 and arm-3 occurrence labels define two permutations relative to arm 1, including when values repeat.  This proves every part of the theorem for rational input; the preceding finite construction and inequalities use only order and finite-dimensional feasibility, and therefore give existence for arbitrary real atoms as well.

Use zero-based indices for the four core atoms and set
\[
 s_{ijk}=A_{1i}+A_{2j}+A_{3k},\qquad
 d_{ijk}=s_{ijk}^2-u_{1i}-u_{2j}-u_{3k}.
\]
For fixed first-coordinate indices \(i=0,1,2,3\), the four exact slack matrices, with rows indexed by \(j\) and columns by \(k\), are
\[
\begin{gathered}
\begin{pmatrix}144&279&479&999\\45&120&260&660\\185&60&0&0\\245&420&660&1260\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}35&0&30&210\\140&45&15&75\\960&665&435&95\\0&5&75&335\end{pmatrix},\\[3pt]
\begin{pmatrix}156&51&11&51\\345&180&80&0\\1445&1080&780&300\\65&0&0&120\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}0&15&95&375\\45&0&20&180\\665&420&240&0\\5&60&180&540\end{pmatrix}.
\end{gathered}
\]
Thus the displayed \(u\)'s are dual feasible for the unshifted squared-sum cost, the smallest positive core slack is \(5\), and the zero-slack cells are
\[
 022,023,101,130,213,231,232,300,311,323.
\]
Give each of the four core atoms marginal count \(m\), and denote the counts on these ten cells in the displayed order by \(t_0,\ldots,t_9\).  The arm-2 label-2 equation minus the arm-1 label-0 equation gives \(t_9=0\).  The arm-3 label-3 and arm-1 label-0 equations then give \(t_4=t_0\).  The arm-2 label-1 and arm-3 label-2 equations give \(t_8=t_6=t_1\).  Subtracting the arm-2 label-3 equation from the arm-1 label-2 equation gives \(t_3=t_4=t_0\).  The arm-1 label-1 and arm-2 label-0 equations give \(t_2=t_1\) and \(t_7=t_0\).  The arm-3 label-0 equation is \(t_3+t_7=m\), hence \(2t_0=m\); finally the arm-1 label-2 equation forces \(t_5=0\).  Since \(t_0+t_1=m\), the unique feasible zero-slack table is
\[
 (t_0,\ldots,t_9)
 =(m/2,m/2,m/2,m/2,m/2,0,m/2,m/2,m/2,0).
\]
For \(m=1\), it has eight positive half-counts.  Directly from the displayed arrays and cells,
\[
 \sum_i u_{1i}+\sum_j u_{2j}+\sum_k u_{3k}=502-207-240=55,
\]
and its primal cost is
\[
 \frac12(4+64+4+1+16+16+4+1)=55.
\]
Thus its unshifted primal and dual objectives both equal \(55\).

Add a dummy atom \((100,100,-200)\) with dual potential zero in each arm.  Mixed cells remain strictly dual-slack.  Indeed, according as the dummy-coordinate set is \(\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\}\), the slack is bounded below respectively by
\[
 71^2,\quad 78^2-184,\quad171^2-184,
 \quad187^2,\quad86^2,\quad85^2-184.
\]
The first value is \(5041\), and every other displayed value is larger.  The all-dummy cell has cost and dual value zero.  Therefore the half-count core table together with \(N-4\) all-dummy rows proves that the unshifted fractional optimum is \(55\).

Any integral completion containing a mixed cell has total dual slack at least \(5041\).  Without a mixed cell, all dummy occurrences form all-dummy rows and the remaining four rows constitute an integral core table.  The unique zero-slack core table above is not integral, so at least one core cell has positive slack, at least \(5\).  Conversely, relative to the first arm, the permutations
\[
 \sigma_2=(2,0,1,3),\qquad \sigma_3=(2,1,3,0)
\]
give rows \(022,101,213,330\) of unshifted squared costs \(4,4,16,36\), totaling \(60=55+5\).  Appending all-dummy rows proves that the unshifted integral optimum is exactly \(60\).

It remains to translate this certificate to the bounded outcomes in def:lower-family.  Their transformed coordinates satisfy
\[
 c_1x_1=\frac{A_1+9}{480},\qquad
 c_2x_2=\frac{A_2+16}{480},\qquad
 c_3x_3=\frac{A_3-7}{480}.
\]
All core and dummy outcomes lie in \([0,1]\).  If \(s\) denotes an unshifted row sum, then the actual row cost is \((s+18)^2/480^2\).  The sum of \(s\) over every feasible coupling is the fixed marginal sum
\[
 \sum_i A_{1i}+\sum_iA_{2i}+\sum_iA_{3i}=-10,
\]
because each dummy row has unshifted sum zero.  Hence every feasible total objective is transformed by
\[
 \sum_{r=1}^N(s_r+18)^2
 =\sum_{r=1}^Ns_r^2+36(-10)+324N.
\]
The fractional and integral total numerators are consequently \(324N-305\) and \(324N-300\).  Division by \(N\cdot480^2=230400N\) gives
\[
 V_{\mathrm{rel}}(F)=\frac{324N-305}{230400N},\qquad
 V_{\mathrm{int}}(F)=\frac{324N-300}{230400N},
\]
and their difference is \(1/(46080N)\), for every \(N\ge4\).  This is an explicit same-class rational witness, with no parity restriction.

For every \(N\ge4\), thm:constructive-rounding-upper and def:worst-gap give
\[
 \Delta_N\le\min\left\{\frac14,\frac{3456}{N}\right\}.
\]
The schedule in thm:explicit-matching-lower is one member of the same scalar class \([0,1]^{3\times N}\), so the supremum in def:worst-gap also satisfies
\[
 \Delta_N\ge\frac1{46080N}.
\]
Both inequalities hold for every integer \(N\ge4\), not merely on a replication subsequence.  Thus \(r_N=N^{-1}\), \(a=1/46080\), and \(b=3456\) certify the sharp asymptotic order and exclude an arithmetic exceptional subsequence for that order.

For \(N=2\), write the two transformed values in arm \(a\) as \(m_a-d_a\) and \(m_a+d_a\), with \(d_a\ge0\).  Any coupling is a law of \(S=(S_1,S_2,S_3)\in\{-1,1\}^3\) satisfying \(\mathbb P(S_a=1)=\mathbb P(S_a=-1)=1/2\); if \(d_a=0\), split the constant atom evenly between its two immaterial sign labels.  Its cost is
\[
 \mathbb E\left[\left(M+\sum_ad_aS_a\right)^2\right]
 =M^2+\mathbb E\left[\left(\sum_ad_aS_a\right)^2\right],
 \qquad M=\sum_am_a,
\]
because every \(S_a\) has mean zero.  Replacing the law by its antipodal symmetrization leaves these marginals and this even objective unchanged.  Every antipodally symmetric law is a convex combination of the four uniform laws on pairs \(\{s,-s\}\).  A linear objective over this simplex is minimized by one such pair, and that pair is exactly a realizable two-row schedule.  Hence \(V_{\mathrm{rel}}(F)=V_{\mathrm{int}}(F)\) for every two-row marginal triple, so \(\Delta_2=0\).

Under ass:complete-randomization the potential-outcome array is fixed and \(Z\) is the sole source of randomness.  Put \(I_{ai}=\mathbf 1\{Z_i=a\}\) and \(Y_{ai}=x_{ai}-\mu_a\).  Since \(\mathbb E I_{ai}=n_a/N\),
\[
 \mathbb E_Z\widehat\theta_N=\sum_ac_a\mu_a=\theta_N.
\]
For distinct units, the fixed-count inclusion probabilities are
\[
 \mathbb E(I_{ai}I_{aj})=\frac{n_a(n_a-1)}{N(N-1)},\qquad
 \mathbb E(I_{ai}I_{bj})=\frac{n_an_b}{N(N-1)}\quad(a\ne b),
\]
whereas \(I_{ai}I_{bi}=0\) for \(a\ne b\).  Define
\[
 S_{ab}=\frac1{N-1}\sum_iY_{ai}Y_{bi},\qquad S_a^2=S_{aa}.
\]
Substitution of the inclusion probabilities into the covariance sums gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_Z\left(n_a^{-1}\sum_iI_{ai}x_{ai}\right)
 =\left(\frac1{n_a}-\frac1N\right)S_a^2,
\]
and, for \(a\ne b\),
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}_Z\left(n_a^{-1}\sum_iI_{ai}x_{ai},
 n_b^{-1}\sum_iI_{bi}x_{bi}\right)=-\frac{S_{ab}}N.
\]
Consequently, with \(\tau_i=\sum_ac_ax_{ai}\), \(\theta_N=N^{-1}\sum_i\tau_i\), and \(S_\tau^2=(N-1)^{-1}\sum_i(\tau_i-\theta_N)^2\),
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\theta_N)
 =\sum_a\frac{c_a^2S_a^2}{n_a}-\frac{S_\tau^2}{N}.
\]
For a completion whose average squared contrast is \(t=N^{-1}\sum_i\tau_i^2\), the fixed marginal moments give
\[
 S_a^2=\frac{N}{N-1}v_a,\quad
 S_\tau^2=\frac{N}{N-1}(t-\theta_N^2).
\]
Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\theta_N)
 =\frac{\sum_a(N/n_a)c_a^2v_a+\theta_N^2-t}{N-1}
 =\frac{B_N(F)-t}{N-1}.
\]

The variance is decreasing in \(t\).  By def:realizable-value, the least realizable \(t\) is \(V_{\mathrm{int}}(F)\), so the sharp upper endpoint is \(U_N(F)\).  The constructed schedule and the relaxation satisfy
\[
 V_{\mathrm{rel}}(F)\le V_{\mathrm{int}}(F)\le C_{\mathrm{alg}}(F),
\]
and hence, by def:variance-certificates,
\[
 U_{\mathrm{lo}}(F)\le U_N(F)\le U_{\mathrm{hi}}(F),
\]
with the exactly computable primal--dual width
\[
 U_{\mathrm{hi}}(F)-U_{\mathrm{lo}}(F)
 =\frac{C_{\mathrm{alg}}(F)-V_{\mathrm{rel}}(F)}{N-1}
 \le\frac{3456}{N(N-1)}.
\]
For \(N\ge4\) the last step is thm:constructive-rounding-upper.  The only remaining feasible three-arm complete-randomization size is \(N=3\); there it follows from \(0\le V_{\mathrm{rel}}(F)\le C_{\mathrm{alg}}(F)\le1/4<3456/3\).  Thus the unrestricted fractional endpoint is an upper certificate; thm:explicit-matching-lower shows explicitly that it need not be realizable by an \(N\)-row completion.

For the lower endpoint, write \(z_{ai}=c_ax_{ai}\).  Expanding the total cost leaves the one-coordinate square sums fixed and gives three pair-product sums:
\[
 \sum_i\left(\sum_az_{ai}\right)^2
 =\sum_{a,i}z_{ai}^2+2\sum_{a<b}\sum_i z_{ai}z_{bi}.
\]
For two sorted sequences \(r_1\le\cdots\le r_N\) and \(s_1\le\cdots\le s_N\), swapping an inversion \(s_j>s_k\) paired to \(r_i<r_l\) changes the product sum by
\[
 (r_is_k+r_ls_j)-(r_is_j+r_ls_k)
 =(r_l-r_i)(s_j-s_k)\ge0.
\]
Repeated swaps prove that equal-rank pairing maximizes every pair-product sum.  Sorting all three \(z\)-columns increasingly attains these three pairwise maxima simultaneously.  For a fractional coupling, each two-coordinate projection is a doubly stochastic fractional pairing; decomposing its flow by the same inversion exchanges gives the identical upper bound.  Hence the comonotone schedule attains the maximum cost both fractionally and realizably, namely \(C_{\max}(F)\).  The variance formula then makes the sharp lower endpoint
\[
 L_N(F)=\frac{B_N(F)-C_{\max}(F)}{N-1}.
\]

For a distribution \(H\) on \([0,1]\), use its nondecreasing quantile \(Q_H\).  The one-dimensional transport identity
\[
 W_1(H,K)=\int_0^1|Q_H(u)-Q_K(u)|\,du
 =\int_0^1|H(t)-K(t)|\,dt
\]
follows for finite laws by matching equal infinitesimal quantile masses and applying \(|r-s|=\int_0^1|\mathbf1\{r\le t\}-\mathbf1\{s\le t\}|\,dt\).  On the interval \(((j-1)/N,j/N]\), monotonicity bounds the integral error from its midpoint value by \(N^{-1}\) times the quantile variation on that interval.  These variations telescope to at most one, so def:plugin-lift gives
\[
 W_1(G_a,\widehat F_a)\le N^{-1}.
\]

Under ass:complete-randomization, arm \(a\) reveals a simple random sample without replacement of size \(n_a\) from the fixed column.  At every \(t\in[0,1]\), the variable \(n_a\widehat F_a(t)\) is hypergeometric.  Direct indicator covariance calculation gives
\[
 \mathbb E\widehat F_a(t)=F_a(t),\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(\widehat F_a(t))
 =\rho_aF_a(t)\{1-F_a(t)\},
 \quad \rho_a=\frac{N-n_a}{n_a(N-1)}.
\]
Tonelli's identity above and Cauchy--Schwarz therefore imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E W_1(\widehat F_a,F_a)
 &=\int_0^1\mathbb E|\widehat F_a(t)-F_a(t)|\,dt\\
 &\le\sqrt{\rho_a}\int_0^1\sqrt{F_a(t)\{1-F_a(t)\}}\,dt
 \le\frac12\sqrt{\rho_a}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The triangle inequality yields \(\mathbb EW_1(G_a,F_a)\le\tfrac12\sqrt{\rho_a}+N^{-1}\).  This calculation is armwise and uses no independence between arms.

We next prove the deterministic perturbation bounds.  If \(X_a,Y_a\in[0,1]\), then both contrasts lie in \([-1/2,1/2]\), whence
\[
 \left|\left(\sum_ac_aX_a\right)^2-
 \left(\sum_ac_aY_a\right)^2\right|
 \le\sum_a|c_a|\,|X_a-Y_a|.
\]
Glue coordinatewise optimal \(W_1\) transports to any coupling of \(F\), conditionally and independently given its coordinates.  The resulting triple has marginals \(G\).  Applying the displayed inequality and then reversing \(F,G\) proves
\[
 |V_{\mathrm{rel}}(F)-V_{\mathrm{rel}}(G)|
 \le\sum_a|c_a|W_1(F_a,G_a).
\]
The same argument with suprema proves this bound for \(C_{\max}\).  When both triples have \(N\) equally weighted occurrences, the sorted coordinatewise matching realizes each \(W_1\); applying its three bijections to an optimal schedule and reversing the roles proves
\[
 |V_{\mathrm{int}}(F)-V_{\mathrm{int}}(G)|
 \le\sum_a|c_a|W_1(F_a,G_a).
\]

Also
\[
 |\mu_a(F)-\mu_a(G)|\le W_1(F_a,G_a).
\]
Since \(v_a(H)=\min_{m\in[0,1]}\int(x-m)^2\,dH(x)\) and \(x\mapsto(x-m)^2\) is uniformly \(2\)-Lipschitz, comparison at the two minimizing means gives
\[
 |v_a(F)-v_a(G)|\le2W_1(F_a,G_a).
\]
Moreover \(|\theta_N(F)|,|\theta_N(G)|\le1/2\), so
\[
 |\theta_N(F)^2-\theta_N(G)^2|
 \le|\theta_N(F)-\theta_N(G)|
 \le\sum_a|c_a|W_1(F_a,G_a).
\]
Combining the last three displays with the definitions of \(B_N,D_N\) and the cost perturbation bounds gives
\[
 |L_N(G)-L_N(F)|\le\frac{D_N(F,G)}{N-1},\qquad
 |U_N(G)-U_N(F)|\le\frac{D_N(F,G)}{N-1}.
\]
Taking expectations in the definition of \(D_N\) gives \(\mathbb ED_N(F,G)\le M_N\).

Apply thm:variance-certificate to \(G\).  Its deterministic rounding width implies
\[
 0\le U_N(G)-U_{\mathrm{lo}}(G)\le\frac{3456}{N(N-1)},
 \qquad
 0\le U_{\mathrm{hi}}(G)-U_N(G)\le\frac{3456}{N(N-1)}.
\]
The triangle inequality therefore proves
\[
 \max\{|U_{\mathrm{lo}}(G)-U_N(F)|,
 |U_{\mathrm{hi}}(G)-U_N(F)|\}
 \le\frac{D_N(F,G)+3456/N}{N-1}.
\]

If \(n_a/N\to p_a\in(0,1)\), then \(\rho_a=O(N^{-1})\), the coefficients in \(D_N\) are bounded, and \(\mathbb ED_N=O(N^{-1/2})+O(N^{-1})\).  Markov's inequality gives \(D_N=O_{\mathbb P}(N^{-1/2})+O(N^{-1})\).  Division by \(N-1\), together with the deterministic rounding term, proves the claimed \(O_{\mathbb P}(N^{-3/2})+O(N^{-2})\) errors for \(L_N(G),U_{\mathrm{lo}}(G),U_{\mathrm{hi}}(G)\).

Finally, for \(\eta\in(0,1)\), Markov's inequality and \(\mathbb ED_N\le M_N\) give
\[
 \mathbb P\{D_N(F,G)\le M_N/\eta\}\ge1-\eta.
\]
On this event the preceding bounds place \(U_N(F)\) inside
\[
 \left[U_{\mathrm{lo}}(G)-\frac{M_N/\eta+3456/N}{N-1},
 U_{\mathrm{hi}}(G)+\frac{M_N/\eta+3456/N}{N-1}\right].
\]
All endpoints and radii in this display are computable from the observed arm samples, the known design sizes, the fractional program, and the deterministic rounding output.

open_obligations.what_is_open: Whether \(\kappa_-=\kappa_+\), the value of a common limit if it exists, and the classification of all asymptotically extremal dual-tight geometries remain open.
open_obligations.obstruction: The handle \(\mathfrak H_{\mathrm{exact}}\) specifies a research program but supplies neither a proved finite obstruction catalogue nor a compactness theorem preserving normalized slack under block decomposition.  The multiscale upper proof loses constants at the cluster-count, residual, and quadratic-charge inequalities, while the padded four-row witness need not maximize any of them.
open_obligations.attempted: The ordered slope intervals were compressed into nested dyadic blocks, residual tables were sparsified and repaired exactly, and the four-row zero-slack face was solved over the reals and integers.  These steps close the uniform rate but provide no matching constant-level variational principle or exclusion of larger irreducible blocks.
open_obligations.partial_result:
The proved frontier gives the nontrivial compact localization
\[
 \frac1{46080}\le \kappa_-\le\kappa_+\le3456.
\]
The lower endpoint is witnessed for every \(N\ge4\) by one fixed four-row obstruction padded with isolated dummy rows, while the upper endpoint follows from the ordered-support multiscale repair.  Thus the order and the absence of an arithmetic exceptional subsequence are settled, but equality of the two asymptotic constants and the classification of all extremal obstruction geometries are not.

proofs.proof_tex:
Write the distinct atoms of \(F_0^{(2)}\) and \(F_1^{(2)}\) as \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_R\) and \(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_S\), respectively, and put
\[
k_r=NF_0^{(2)}(\{\alpha_r\}),\qquad
\ell_s=NF_1^{(2)}(\{\beta_s\}).
\]
Because both laws are empirical laws of \(N\) fixed entries, every \(k_r\) and \(\ell_s\) is a positive integer and
\(\sum_r k_r=\sum_s\ell_s=N\).  Every coupling in \(\Gamma(F^{(2)})\) is supported on the finite Cartesian product of these atom sets.  Thus it is represented by a nonnegative matrix \(p=(p_{rs})\) satisfying
\[
\sum_s p_{rs}=\frac{k_r}{N},\qquad
\sum_r p_{rs}=\frac{\ell_s}{N}.
\]
After the invertible scaling \(q=Np\), the feasible set is the transportation polytope
\[
q_{rs}\geq 0,\qquad \sum_s q_{rs}=k_r,\qquad \sum_r q_{rs}=\ell_s. \tag{1}
\]

We first prove the required integrality rather than assume a transportation-polytope theorem.  Associate with a feasible \(q\) the bipartite graph having a row vertex \(r\), a column vertex \(s\), and an edge \((r,s)\) exactly when \(q_{rs}>0\).  If this positive-support graph contains a cycle, assign alternating signs \(+1,-1,+1,-1,\ldots\) to its edges and zero off the cycle.  The resulting matrix \(h\neq0\) has every row and column sum equal to zero.  Taking
\(0<\varepsilon<\min\{q_{rs}:(r,s)\text{ lies on the cycle}\}\) gives two distinct feasible matrices \(q+\varepsilon h\) and \(q-\varepsilon h\) whose midpoint is \(q\).  Hence the support of every extreme point is a forest.

Now let \(q\) be an extreme point.  In each nonempty component of its support forest, choose a leaf.  The weight on the unique edge incident to that leaf equals the leaf's residual margin in (1), which is an integer.  Delete that edge and leaf and subtract this integer weight from the neighboring residual margin.  The new residual margins remain nonnegative integers.  Iterating, while discarding any isolated zero-margin vertex, shows that every positive entry of \(q\) is an integer.  Expanding the cell \((r,s)\) into \(q_{rs}\) rows \((\alpha_r,\beta_s)\) produces exactly \(N\) rows and uses \(\alpha_r\) exactly \(k_r\) times and \(\beta_s\) exactly \(\ell_s\) times.  It therefore produces a member of \(\mathcal S_N(F^{(2)})\).  This proves that every extreme point of \(\Gamma(F^{(2)})\) is realizable.

The polytope (1) is nonempty, because \(q_{rs}=k_r\ell_s/N\) is feasible, and it is closed and bounded in a finite-dimensional space.  The linear cost therefore has a minimizer and a maximizer.  Starting from either optimizer, if its positive support contains a cycle, use the alternating perturbation above and increase \(\varepsilon\) until an edge first becomes zero.  Linearity says that the original objective is the average of the two perturbed objectives.  At a minimum both perturbed objectives are no smaller, so both equal the original objective; at a maximum the reversed inequalities give the same conclusion.  Retaining a perturbed optimizer with one fewer positive cell and iterating produces an acyclic, hence integral, optimizer.  Thus both extrema may be computed over \(\mathcal S_N(F^{(2)})\).  It remains to identify them.  Since \(d_0+d_1=0\), write \(d=(\lambda,-\lambda)\), where the case \(\lambda=0\) is included.  Expand the two empirical marginals into ordered lists
\[
A_1\leq\cdots\leq A_N,\qquad B_1\leq\cdots\leq B_N.
\]
After using the first list as row labels, every realizable table has cost
\[
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N(\lambda A_i-\lambda B_{\sigma(i)})^2
=\frac{\lambda^2}{N}\left(\sum_i A_i^2+\sum_iB_i^2-2\sum_iA_iB_{\sigma(i)}\right) \tag{2}
\]
for a permutation \(\sigma\).  If \(i<j\), \(A_i\leq A_j\), and the two paired values satisfy \(B_{\sigma(i)}>B_{\sigma(j)}\), swapping those two values changes the product sum by
\[
(A_iB_{\sigma(j)}+A_jB_{\sigma(i)})
 -(A_iB_{\sigma(i)}+A_jB_{\sigma(j)})
=(A_j-A_i)(B_{\sigma(i)}-B_{\sigma(j)})\geq0. \tag{3}
\]
Successively removing inversions proves that \(\sum_iA_iB_{\sigma(i)}\) is maximized by like ordering.  Applying the same exchange argument to \(-B_i\), or equivalently successively removing like-ordered pairs, proves that it is minimized by reverse ordering.  Equalities in (3) show that repeated atoms cause no problem.  Since each empirical quantile is constant on intervals of length \(1/N\), equation (2) now gives
\[
\min_{\pi\in\Gamma(F^{(2)})}\int(d_0y_0+d_1y_1)^2\,d\pi
=\int_0^1[d_0Q_0^{(2)}(u)+d_1Q_1^{(2)}(u)]^2\,du
=C_{\mathrm{co}}^{(2)}(F^{(2)}), \tag{4}
\]
and, with identities at the finitely many quantile boundaries irrelevant to the integral,
\[
\max_{\pi\in\Gamma(F^{(2)})}\int(d_0y_0+d_1y_1)^2\,d\pi
=\int_0^1[d_0Q_0^{(2)}(u)+d_1Q_1^{(2)}(1-u)]^2\,du
=C_{\mathrm{ctr}}^{(2)}(F^{(2)}). \tag{5}
\]
The same extrema over \(\mathcal S_N(F^{(2)})\) follow from integrality.

We next derive the design variance.  Fix any table \(T\in\mathcal S_N(F^{(2)})\), and let
\[
I_{bi}=\mathbf 1\{Z_i^{(2)}=b\},\qquad
S_{10}^{(2)}(T)=\frac1{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N(T_{1i}-\mu_1^{(2)})(T_{0i}-\mu_0^{(2)}).
\]
The complete-randomization assumption and positivity of \(m_0,m_1\) give
\[
\mathbb E I_{bi}=\frac{m_b}{N},\qquad
\mathbb E(I_{bi}I_{bj})=\frac{m_b(m_b-1)}{N(N-1)}\quad(i\ne j), \tag{6}
\]
and
\[
\mathbb E(I_{0i}I_{1i})=0,\qquad
\mathbb E(I_{0i}I_{1j})=\frac{m_0m_1}{N(N-1)}\quad(i\ne j). \tag{7}
\]
In particular,
\[
\mathbb E_{Z^{(2)}}\widehat\theta_N^{(2)}
=\sum_{b\in\mathbb B}\frac{d_b}{m_b}\sum_i\frac{m_b}{N}T_{bi}
=\sum_{b\in\mathbb B}d_b\mu_b^{(2)}
=\theta_N^{(2)}, \tag{8}
\]
so the estimator is design-unbiased for the fixed causal contrast.

For completeness, center \(T_{bi}\) at \(\mu_b^{(2)}\).  Using (6), the facts that the centered entries sum to zero and that their squared sum is \((N-1)S_b^{2,(2)}\) yield
\[
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac1{m_b}\sum_i I_{bi}T_{bi}\right)
=\left(\frac1{m_b}-\frac1N\right)S_b^{2,(2)}. \tag{9}
\]
Likewise, (7) and
\[
\sum_{i\ne j}(T_{0i}-\mu_0^{(2)})(T_{1j}-\mu_1^{(2)})
=-\sum_i(T_{0i}-\mu_0^{(2)})(T_{1i}-\mu_1^{(2)})
\]
give
\[
\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\frac1{m_0}\sum_iI_{0i}T_{0i},
\frac1{m_1}\sum_iI_{1i}T_{1i}\right)
=-\frac1N S_{10}^{(2)}(T). \tag{10}
\]
Combining (9)--(10),
\[
\operatorname{Var}_{Z^{(2)}}(\widehat\theta_N^{(2)})
=\sum_{b\in\mathbb B}\frac{d_b^2S_b^{2,(2)}}{m_b}
-\frac1N\left\{\sum_{b\in\mathbb B}d_b^2S_b^{2,(2)}
+2d_0d_1S_{10}^{(2)}(T)\right\}. \tag{11}
\]
Define the fixed row contrast \(\tau_i=d_0T_{0i}+d_1T_{1i}\) and its average squared value
\(C_T=N^{-1}\sum_i\tau_i^2\).  Its mean is \(\theta_N^{(2)}\), because the marginal means do not depend on \(T\).  Therefore
\[
\frac1{N-1}\sum_i(\tau_i-\theta_N^{(2)})^2
=\frac{N}{N-1}\{C_T-(\theta_N^{(2)})^2\}
=\sum_b d_b^2S_b^{2,(2)}+2d_0d_1S_{10}^{(2)}(T). \tag{12}
\]
Since \(S_b^{2,(2)}=Nv_b^{(2)}/(N-1)\), substituting (12) into (11) gives the exact cost representation
\[
\operatorname{Var}_{Z^{(2)}}(\widehat\theta_N^{(2)})
=\frac{1}{N-1}\left\{
\sum_{b\in\mathbb B}\frac{N}{m_b}d_b^2v_b^{(2)}
+(\theta_N^{(2)})^2-C_T\right\}
=\frac{B_N^{(2)}(F^{(2)})-C_T}{N-1}. \tag{13}
\]

The first term in the numerator of (13) depends only on the fixed marginals.  Thus (4)--(5) imply that the maximum design variance over \(\mathcal S_N(F^{(2)})\) is obtained by the comonotone table and the minimum by the countermonotone table.  The schedule class is finite, so both extrema are attained; hence the interval hull is exactly
\[
\left[
\frac{B_N^{(2)}(F^{(2)})-C_{\mathrm{ctr}}^{(2)}(F^{(2)})}{N-1},
\frac{B_N^{(2)}(F^{(2)})-C_{\mathrm{co}}^{(2)}(F^{(2)})}{N-1}
\right]
=\bigl[L_N^{(2)}(F^{(2)}),U_N^{(2)}(F^{(2)})\bigr], \tag{14}
\]
where the last equality is exactly \(\mathrm{def:two-arm-endpoints}\).

Finally, expanding the comonotone cost around the two marginal means gives
\[
\frac{N}{N-1}\left\{C_{\mathrm{co}}^{(2)}(F^{(2)})-(\theta_N^{(2)})^2\right\}
=\sum_b d_b^2S_b^{2,(2)}+2d_0d_1\overline S_{10}^{(2)}, \tag{15}
\]
because
\(\overline S_{10}^{(2)}=\frac{N}{N-1}\{\int_0^1Q_1^{(2)}(u)Q_0^{(2)}(u)\,du-\mu_1^{(2)}\mu_0^{(2)}\}\).
The identical expansion with \(Q_1^{(2)}(1-u)\) gives
\[
\frac{N}{N-1}\left\{C_{\mathrm{ctr}}^{(2)}(F^{(2)})-(\theta_N^{(2)})^2\right\}
=\sum_b d_b^2S_b^{2,(2)}+2d_0d_1\underline S_{10}^{(2)}. \tag{16}
\]
Substitution of (15)--(16) into (13)--(14) proves
\[
U_N^{(2)}
=\sum_b\frac{d_b^2S_b^{2,(2)}}{m_b}
-\frac{\sum_b d_b^2S_b^{2,(2)}+2d_0d_1\overline S_{10}^{(2)}}{N},
\]
and
\[
L_N^{(2)}
=\sum_b\frac{d_b^2S_b^{2,(2)}}{m_b}
-\frac{\sum_b d_b^2S_b^{2,(2)}+2d_0d_1\underline S_{10}^{(2)}}{N}.
\]
These are the scaled-contrast versions of the sharp endpoints in Aronow, Green, and Lee (2014, Lemma~1 and equations~(7)--(11)); the argument above independently derives them from the stated complete-randomization law and the fixed empirical marginals.
